The `STM32` high-speed analog acquisition system suffered buffer overrun errors during continuous sampling because the `DMA` cyclic buffer handler failed to service half-transfer interrupts before the transfer-complete flag asserted. The circular `DMA` channel pushed 12-bit `ADC` samples into a 512-byte ring buffer in static `RAM` at 2 megasamples per second. Logic analyzer captures revealed that the interrupt service routine stalled on a mutex lock for 48 microseconds, which caused the peripheral `DMA` controller to overwrite unprocessed samples.

Telemetry traces confirmed that the circular buffer pointer wrapped around before core 0 cleared the half-transfer interrupt pending flag in the status register. We isolated the timing bottleneck by profiling the direct memory access event queue under heavy load.

We eliminated the cyclic buffer overruns by replacing the blocking mutex with double-buffered circular memory pointers and splitting the processing workload across ping-pong buffers. We also updated the `DMA` control register by setting the circular mode enable bit and clearing the transfer error interrupt mask to maintain continuous streaming without frame loss.

The `RP2040` embedded device failed `USB` descriptor enumeration during host connection because the `USB` device controller corrupted endpoint buffer descriptors during control transfer transactions. When the host requested the 64-byte device descriptor packet at `USB` address 0, the hardware state machine attempted to load descriptor bytes from unaligned static `RAM`. `Wireshark` protocol traces showed that the host controller issued 3 consecutive get descriptor requests and reset the bus after receiving truncated stall responses.

Hardware register inspection revealed that the endpoint control register cleared the buffer ready bit prematurely while the `DMA` controller was still writing the descriptor data packet. The host transceiver detected a packet length mismatch on endpoint 0 and flagged an invalid transaction error within 16 milliseconds.

We resolved the enumeration failure by aligning the `USB` descriptor table on a 256-byte boundary in dedicated dual-port `USB` `RAM`. We also updated the endpoint buffer initialization sequence by verifying the buffer available bit before arming control transfer responses, which allows the host to complete device enumeration at 12 megabits per second.

The `ESP32` environmental datalogger crashed during flash wear leveling operations because the non-volatile storage partition driver exhausted available erase blocks in the active flash sector. The storage subsystem logged sensor telemetry every 10 seconds, writing 128 bytes to `SPI` flash memory until the wear-leveling cycle counter surpassed 90000 erase cycles on the primary partition. `J-Link` debugger traces showed that the wear leveling engine attempted to rotate modified metadata into a retired block marked with a bad sector flag.

Telemetry confirmed that the flash memory controller triggered an unhandled cache error exception when reading block headers across erased sector boundaries. Because the driver failed to allocate a spare swap block from the wear-leveling pool, core 0 entered a panic loop while holding the flash translation table lock.

We resolved the flash wear leveling crash by expanding the wear-leveling reserve partition to 4 dedicated swap sectors in external flash memory. We also updated the non-volatile storage driver by implementing dynamic wear distribution across physical sectors and clearing stale block markers before writing updated allocation tables.

The `nRF52` wireless sensor beacon suffered premature battery depletion because the low-power analog comparator generated spurious wake-up interrupts during system deep sleep. The battery monitoring circuit tracked supply rail voltage fluctuations through an external analog input pin tied to the internal comparator peripheral. Oscilloscope measurements showed that high-frequency switching noise on the power rail induced 24 millivolts of ripple, which crossed the comparator reference threshold and woke the processor every 8 milliseconds.

Hardware trace logs revealed that the comparator event register asserted the wake-up flag without digital hysteresis filtering enabled in peripheral control registers. This unintended wake-up cycle prevented the system power management module from staying in 2-microamp sleep mode.

We fixed the excessive power depletion by configuring the low-power comparator hysteresis register with a 50-millivolt window and routing the reference input through an internal low-pass filter. We also modified the power manager interrupt handler by clearing pending comparator events before entering sleep, which stabilized the standby current at 3 microamps.

The `RISC-V` powertrain microcontroller dropped `CAN-FD` communication frames during high speed bitrate switching because the transceiver transmitter delay compensation offset was miscalculated in the peripheral timing registers. When the `CAN-FD` controller switched from the nominal 1 megabit arbitration phase to the 5 megabit data payload phase, the loop delay between the transmit pin and receive pin exceeded the configured secondary sample point. `Wireshark` CAN bus traces captured 64 consecutive bit error flags caused by sample point mismatch during data frame transmission.

Diagnostic logs showed that the `CAN` controller asserted the error passive interrupt after the transmit error counter climbed past 128 events. The transceiver delay measurement unit recorded an internal propagation delay of 180 nanoseconds, while the delay compensation register remained fixed at 40 nanoseconds.

We corrected the bitrate switching failures by programming the transmitter delay compensation offset register to 160 nanoseconds in the `CAN-FD` core. We also adjusted the data phase prescaler and nominal bit timing registers by shifting the secondary sample point to 75 percent, which eliminated bus arbitration drops and restored reliable frame transmission.
